new_statements.quote: Most conspicuous among the many developments which characterize Northern Paman reflection of Proto Paman is the reduction of initial syllables (*CV1) by loss of initial consonants (*C1) and loss or other reduction of immediately following vowels (*V1). Associated with initial reduction, and at least partially responsible for it is a shift of primary stress (a strictly phonetic feature) from the initial to the second syllable (*CV2) in Paman stems. In all Northern Paman languages, except Uraði and its sister dialects, *C1 was lost invariably. [...] Short *V1 was lost in some languages, retained in others, and metathesized in still others.

Associated with initial reduction, and at least partia…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level statement by the fieldworker covering all his Northern Paman varieties, Ŋkot̠ = Ngkoth included: primary stress is non-contrastive ('strictly phonetic') and sits on the reflex of the Proto-Paman second syllable, the old initial syllable having been reduced (initial consonant lost invariably in Ngkoth; initial short vowel lost, kept or metathesised). Synchronically this amounts to stress on the first consonant-initial syllable of the modern word (word-initial in the now common cluster-initial/monosyllabic stems, second syllable in vowel-initial words), which is exactly the rule Hale states explicitly for the sister language Linngithigh on p. 179 ('the first vowel which is preceded by a consonant is stressed'); Hale gives no separate synchronic stress rule for Ngkoth itself, either here or in the Ngkot section of his 1976a paper.
new_statements.exceptions: Uradhi and its sister dialects are excepted only with respect to invariable *C1 loss, not explicitly with respect to the stress shift; no Ngkoth-specific exceptions.
new_statements.domain_note: Diachronic/comparative statement about 'Paman stems' (word level); stress called 'a strictly phonetic feature', i.e. non-phonemic. No phrase-level information. Ngkoth data from one consultant (Frank Moreton), Weipa 1960.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is Hale's own first-hand generalisation over the whole Northern Paman subgroup (Glottolog nort2758 'Northern Paman'), of which Ŋkot̠ (= Ngkoth, ngko1236; consultant Frank Moreton, Weipa 1960) is one of his 13 sampled varieties (listed AL 8(2):163, described 165-166). It is not an Ngkoth-specific synchronic rule; Hale's Ngkot section in the fuller 1976a paper lists five 'major phonological developments' and none concerns stress. The only explicit synchronic stress rule Hale gives for a Northern Paman language in this source is for the sister language Linngithigh (linn1234), p. 179.

Voegelin, Languages of the World: Indo-Pacific Fascicle Six. Anthropological Linguistics 8(2): 1-197, at pp. 162-197. (ERIC ED 010 364 microfiche; archive.org micro_IA41153350_0264)
sources.note: pp. 167-168: in Northern Paman (all sampled languages incl. Ŋkot̠) primary stress, 'a strictly phonetic feature', shifted from the initial to the second syllable (*CV2) of Paman stems, associated with and partly responsible for loss of *C1 (invariable in all NP languages except Uradhi) and loss/reduction of *V1. Ŋkot̠ entry pp. 165-166 gives location/dialects only. p. 179 gives an explicit synchronic rule for sister language Linngithigh: the first vowel preceded by a consonant is stressed.
